youtube_description:
Takenaka Hanbee was too frail to fight, too sick to survive his thirties, and yet Toyotomi Hideyoshi called him one of the two minds behind his rise to power. From a stunning castle takeover as a young man to a war camp he refused to leave while dying, this is the story of a strategist history almost forgot to write down.

scenes.narration: He had weeks left to live. He spent them planning another man's war. What could matter more than survival?

scenes.narration: Takenaka Hanbee Shigeharu was born in 1544 in Mino Province, heir to a minor fortress at Bodaisan. From childhood he was frail — pale, slight, prone to illness in an age that measured a warrior's worth in brute strength. He could not out-fight the soldiers around him, and by most accounts never tried to. What set him apart was different: an unusual patience for reading a battlefield, a mind that noticed the detail everyone else missed. In a province sliding toward collapse under a careless young lord, that quiet intelligence would soon matter far more than any sword.

Unlike the training soldiers (who have the standard shaved-forehead sakayaki samurai hairstyle), the boy's hair completely covers his entire head with no shaved patch anywhere — full unshaved hairline, combed straight back, a young child's version of the sōhatsu court-noble style he will keep his whole life. Autumn mist clings to the surrounding hills. His posture is still and observant, visibly less robust than the young men training beyond him.

scenes.narration: By the early 1560s, Mino Province was ruled by Saito Tatsuoki, grandson of the fearsome Saito Dosan. Tatsuoki had inherited a formidable domain and, in the judgment of nearly every chronicler since, none of the discipline needed to hold it. He surrounded himself with favorites, ignored his senior retainers, and let the business of governing slide while rival warlords circled. Among those retainers was young Hanbee, watching his lord's negligence with the same close attention he brought to everything else. To the south, Oda Nobunaga was already eyeing Mino's rich farmland. Inside the province, patience with Tatsuoki was running out.

scenes.narration: In 1564, Hanbee did something no one expected of the quiet, sickly retainer. With a handful of men — some accounts say fewer than twenty — he and his father-in-law slipped into Inabayama Castle, Mino's mountain capital, and seized it outright while their lord was away. It was one of the boldest single acts of the entire Sengoku period, and to this day historians debate why he did it. Was it rebellion? Or was it, as some traditions claim, a desperate lesson aimed at a lord too careless to notice his own castle could fall to a handful of men?
scenes.image_prompt: Under cover of night, a small band of samurai led by a slight, pale strategist in plain dark robes scales the mountain approach to a formidable hilltop castle, moving past unsuspecting sentries toward the gate. The leading strategist's hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere (sōhatsu style like a Heian-period court noble, NOT the sakayaki-shaved-forehead look of the samurai following him) — full unshaved hairline, hair combed straight back and tied at the nape. Torchlight flickers against stone walls. The scene conveys tense, quiet audacity rather than open combat — a handful of men against an entire fortress.

scenes.narration: Whatever Hanbee's true motive, his next move was stranger still. After holding Inabayama for roughly half a year — long enough to make his point unmistakable — he simply handed the castle back to Tatsuoki and withdrew to private life at Bodaisan. He had proven he could topple his own lord's capital almost effortlessly, then walked away from the power that act might have bought him. No surviving record explains the decision in his own words. It left behind only a reputation: a man capable of extraordinary things, who did not appear to want what most men fought a lifetime to seize.

The strategist's hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere (sōhatsu style like a Heian-period court noble, NOT the sakayaki-shaved-forehead look of the watching soldiers) — full unshaved hairline, hair combed straight back and tied at the nape. No legible writing anywhere.

scenes.narration: In 1567, Oda Nobunaga finally broke Mino's defenses and took Inabayama Castle for himself, renaming it Gifu. Tatsuoki's rule was over. Hanbee, now a private citizen with an extraordinary reputation, drew the attention of one of Nobunaga's rising commanders: Kinoshita Tokichiro, the future Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Later tradition holds that Hideyoshi visited Hanbee's mountain retreat three times before the reclusive strategist agreed to serve him — a story often compared to the legendary recruitment of the Chinese strategist Zhuge Liang. Whether that detail is fact or later embellishment is impossible to confirm. What is certain is that Hanbee, once persuaded, never served anyone else.

Picture a modern man with an ordinary full head of straight black hair combed straight back with no part, just tied back in a low tail at the nape — that is exactly what the top and front of his head looks like. This is completely different from the commander's shaved-forehead sakayaki look beside him. Autumn leaves scatter across the path between them. The mood is one of quiet persistence meeting quiet reluctance.

scenes.narration: Hanbee entered Hideyoshi's service not as a soldier but as a gunshi — a strategist whose weapon was information rather than steel. He rode with Hideyoshi through the Oda campaigns of the following years, against the Asakura in Echizen and the Azai in northern Omi, offering counsel on sieges, terrain, and timing rather than leading charges himself. Contemporaries who watched him work noted a man who rarely raised his voice and rarely needed to: when Hanbee spoke in council, commanders listened, because his read of a situation was so often, uncannily, correct. His body remained frail. His judgment did not.

scenes.narration: Within Hideyoshi's growing command, Hanbee occupied an unusual position. He carried no famous blade, wore no ostentatious armor, and rarely appeared on the front line of a charge. Where other retainers built reputations through personal combat, Hanbee built his through results that were harder to see and harder to dispute: castles that fell without a costly assault, enemies maneuvered into surrender before the fighting began. It was a different kind of courage — the willingness to be judged entirely by outcomes rather than by how a man looked in the moment of battle. Hideyoshi came to depend on him completely.

scenes.narration: In 1577, Hideyoshi was given a new and enormous assignment: subdue the Mori clan and the whole of western Japan on Nobunaga's behalf. It was a campaign that would be won less through open battle than through siege — surrounding fortress after fortress, cutting supply lines, and forcing surrender through starvation and pressure rather than storm. This was precisely the kind of warfare Hanbee had always favored, patient and calculating rather than reckless. As Hideyoshi's forces pushed into Harima Province, his sickly strategist worked alongside a second advisor whose methods matched his own.

The map carries no legible writing or place names. Outside the tent, an army's watchfires stretch toward the western horizon.

scenes.narration: In 1578, disaster struck. A senior Oda commander rebelled at Itami Castle, and Hideyoshi sent his fellow strategist to negotiate — only for the man to vanish behind the rebel's walls, imprisoned and presumed a traitor. Nobunaga, believing the advisor had defected, ordered the man's young son executed, and the order came down through Hideyoshi's camp. Hanbee intervened. He is said to have quietly hidden the boy instead of carrying out the order, insisting his colleague's loyalty could not be so easily doubted. It was a lie told to the most dangerous man in Japan. The prisoner behind those walls would not go free for more than a year — long enough that Hanbee never lived to see his gamble vindicated.

The strategist's hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere (sōhatsu style like a Heian-period court noble, NOT the standard sakayaki-shaved-forehead samurai look) — full unshaved hairline, hair combed straight back and tied at the nape. Dim lantern light, tense but protective atmosphere.

scenes.narration: By 1578, Hanbee's own body was failing. The illness that had shadowed him since childhood — a wasting sickness of the chest, likely what would later be recognized as tuberculosis — was tightening its grip with every passing month in the field. Campaign life offered no rest: damp winter sieges, long marches, sleepless councils. Retainers who served alongside him noticed the change — the coughing he tried to hide, the frame growing thinner beneath his robes. Hideyoshi noticed too. And yet, as the campaign against the Mori intensified through 1578 and into 1579, Hanbee did not ask to be relieved of duty.
scenes.image_prompt: Inside a spare siege-camp tent at night, a gaunt strategist sits hunched over unrolled maps by lamplight, one hand pressed briefly to his chest as he suppresses a cough, his frame visibly thinner than in earlier scenes. His hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere (sōhatsu style like a Heian-period court noble, NOT the standard sakayaki-shaved-forehead samurai look) — full unshaved hairline, hair combed straight back and tied at the nape. An ink brush and unfinished notes lie scattered around him, the maps and papers bearing no legible writing or place names. The mood is quiet determination against visible physical decline.

scenes.narration: The campaign's hardest test came at Miki Castle, where Hideyoshi's forces settled in for a siege designed to starve the fortress into submission rather than storm it — a strategy built on exactly the patient calculation Hanbee had spent his career refining. But by the spring of 1579, his illness had become impossible to ignore. Hideyoshi sent him back to Kyoto for treatment, away from the cold and damp of the siege camp. Hanbee went. And then, within weeks, he came back. He is said to have insisted that a strategist's place was beside his lord's army until the work was done — that if he was going to die anyway, he would rather die in the field than in a quiet room far away.

The strategist stands facing the camera-left, three-quarter view of his face and forehead clearly visible: his forehead is completely covered in hair down to his eyebrows, with no shaved skin visible on his forehead or the top of his head at all — think of a modern man's hairline, full and unshaved, combed straight back close to the scalp, ending in a small low-hanging tail at the nape, WITHOUT any bun, knot, or hair mass piled on top of or above his head. He shakes his head calmly, one hand already resting on a spread map bearing no legible writing, refusing to leave again. Firelight and tension fill the small space between them.

scenes.narration: Once back, Hanbee did not leave the siege lines again. Through the spring of 1579 he went on advising the blockade of Miki Castle from his camp quarters, his health visibly collapsing around him. On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of 1579 — the sixth of July on the Western calendar — Takenaka Hanbee died at Hideyoshi's camp on Hirai Hill outside Miki, still within reach of the war he had spent a decade shaping from the shadows. He was thirty-six by the Japanese count of his day. The siege he had helped design would grind on for another seven months after his death, exactly as he had planned it — a campaign that outlived the man who conceived it.

scenes.narration: In January 1580, Miki Castle finally surrendered, starved into submission after a siege so total that later generations would call it 'Miki no Hoshigoroshi' — the starving of Miki. It was a victory built almost entirely on the patient, bloodless strategy Hanbee had championed throughout his career: a fortress broken not by storming its walls, but by controlling everything outside them until surrender became the only option left. Hideyoshi had lost the strategist who designed the campaign months before he saw it succeed. What remained was the method itself, carried forward by the commanders he had trained.

The victorious army stands in disciplined formation, plain unmarked banners lowered rather than triumphant and carrying no lettering, conveying exhaustion and quiet resolution rather than celebration.

scenes.narration: The fellow strategist Hanbee had once saved was not pulled out of the Itami dungeon until late 1579 — months after Hanbee was already dead. He learned only then the full extent of what had been done for him: a son hidden from execution, a loyalty vouched for while Nobunaga himself had condemned it. The two men, so often paired in later memory as Hideyoshi's twin minds, had barely overlapped in the field before illness took one of them. The survivor would go on to serve Hideyoshi for nearly two more decades. Hanbee never saw the empire his strategy helped build — only the siege lines outside one castle, to the very end.

Muted grey morning light, no other figures present, a solemn and reflective atmosphere.

scenes.narration: In the centuries that followed, storytellers gave Hanbee a title borrowed from Chinese history: 'Ima Komei' — the Kongming of his age, a living echo of Zhuge Liang, the most celebrated strategist in Chinese tradition. It is a striking comparison, and a useful one for legend. It is also, by most modern scholarship, difficult to trace to any source from Hanbee's own lifetime. What survives in contemporary records is more modest and, in its way, more remarkable: a physically frail retainer, never a great warrior, whose counsel shaped campaigns across an entire province-conquering war — without needing the myth to make the case for him.

A faded, aged portrait scroll is propped nearby depicting a slight, pale strategist whose hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere, combed straight back into a low tail at the nape (sōhatsu style, like a Heian-period court noble) — no legible writing visible on any surface. The scene conveys legend being written down long after the events it describes.

scenes.narration: Hanbee and his fellow strategist together became known to later generations as Hideyoshi's 'Ryobee' — the two Bee, named for the ending both their names happened to share, both of them indispensable to his rise. It is a tidy pairing, and a popular one in the centuries of fiction that followed the Sengoku period. Whether the two men saw themselves that way, or were simply two capable advisors who briefly crossed paths in a decade-long campaign, the surviving record does not say. What it does confirm is that Hideyoshi's later success rested on minds like theirs at least as much as on any army he commanded.

scenes.narration: Separating the historical Takenaka Hanbee from the legend built around him afterward is not straightforward. The Inabayama takeover, the three visits from Hideyoshi, the Ima Komei title, the tidy symmetry with his fellow strategist — each carries the fingerprints of storytellers writing generations later, shaping a difficult, undocumented life into something more satisfying than uncertainty usually allows. What can be said with more confidence is narrower, and in some ways more compelling: a chronically ill man who chose strategy over survival, repeatedly, in a century that rewarded neither patience nor mercy, and who was trusted with decisions that determined who lived and who did not.

scenes.narration: Look closely at the two moments Hanbee is best remembered for, and a pattern appears. As a young man, he seized his own lord's castle to make a point no one wanted to hear, then walked away from the power it offered. As a dying man, he walked away from the comfort his lord had arranged for him and came back to the siege, choosing a war camp over a sickbed because the work mattered more than his own survival. Both times, Hanbee did exactly what he judged necessary and nothing more — indifferent to what people expected a man in his position to want.

In both halves, the strategist's hair completely covers his entire head with zero shaved patches anywhere (sōhatsu style like a Heian-period court noble, NOT the standard sakayaki-shaved-forehead samurai look) — full unshaved hairline, hair combed straight back and tied at the nape, consistent at both ages. Soft matching light ties both halves of the image together, no legible writing anywhere.

scenes.narration: Takenaka Hanbee is remembered today less as a conqueror than as a mind that shaped conquest from just outside the frame — planning battles he would never personally win glory in, advising a lord who would go on to rule Japan without him. He died young, largely unheralded in his own time, and became, centuries later, one of the most quietly celebrated strategists in Japanese history. It's the kind of story that rewards a second look — and if this one did, there are more like it waiting for you here.
